In [[group theory]], a [[subgroup]] <math>H</math> of a [[group (mathematics)|group]] <math>G</math> is termed '''malnormal''' if for any group element <math>x</math> not in <math>H</math>, <math>H</math> and <math>xHx^{-1}</math> [[intersection (set theory)|intersect]] only in the [[identity element]].{{sfnp|Lyndon|Schupp|2001|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=aiPVBygHi_oC&pg=PA203 203]}}

Some facts about malnormality:

* The intersection of malnormal subgroups is malnormal.{{sfnp|Gildenhuys|Kharlampovich|Myasnikov|1995}}

* Malnormality is [[transitive relation|transitive]]; that is, a malnormal subgroup of a malnormal subgroup is malnormal.{{sfnp|Karrass|Solitar|1971}}

* The trivial subgroup and the whole group are malnormal subgroups. A [[normal subgroup]] that is also malnormal must be one of these.{{sfnp|de la Harpe|Weber|2014}}

* Every malnormal subgroup is a special type of [[C-group]] called a trivial intersection subgroup, or TI subgroup.

When <math>G</math> is [[finite group|finite]], a malnormal subgroup <math>H</math> distinct from 1 and <math>G</math> is called a "Frobenius complement".{{sfnp|de la Harpe|Weber|2014}} The set <math>N</math> of elements of <math>G</math> which are either equal to 1 or non-conjugate to any element of <math>H</math> is a normal subgroup of <math>G</math>, called the "Frobenius kernel", and <math>G</math> is the [[semidirect product]] of <math>H</math> and <math>N</math>.{{sfnp|Feit|1967|pp=133–139}}
